connection: Sessions 01 and 02 established the project layout and dependency direction. This session returns to the real console application and uses its build-run-test loop to observe how names, types, literals, conversions, and expressions produce values.
objectives: Describe a variable as a typed name bound to a value, not as an untyped box.
Distinguish declarations, literals, conversions, and expressions.
Choose decimal for deliberate base-10 quantities and recognize when a conversion is explicit.
Predict the value and type produced by a small numeric expression.

visuals.title: A name carries a type contract
visuals.explanation: The variable name hours makes intent visible, while its declared type limits which values and operations are valid.

visuals.title: Expressions produce values
visuals.explanation: Operands and operators are evaluated to produce a result. The result can be assigned, passed, returned, or observed.

visuals.title: Types control valid operations
visuals.explanation: A value must fit the target type. When types differ, C# either applies a permitted implicit conversion or requires an explicit cast.

visuals.title: Decimal models base-10 quantities
visuals.explanation: decimal is useful when base-10 precision is part of the domain. The m suffix makes a numeric literal a decimal value.

preQuiz.prompt: What does the m suffix mean in 8m?
options: The value is measured in meters
preQuiz.explanation: The suffix tells the compiler to treat the literal as decimal.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does converting TotalHours to decimal require an explicit cast?
options: TotalHours is a double and the conversion can change representation
preQuiz.explanation: double and decimal use different representations, so C# requires the programmer to acknowledge this conversion.

preQuiz.prompt: If recordedHours is 8m and scheduledHours is 7.5m, what does recordedHours - scheduledHours produce?
preQuiz.explanation: Subtraction evaluates both decimal operands and produces a decimal result.

concept.title: Declarations create typed names
paragraphs: A declaration connects a type, a name, and usually an initial value. The type is a compile-time contract: it determines which values can be assigned and which operations are available.
Names should explain the role a value plays. scheduledHours communicates more than x even when both have the same type.

concept.title: Expressions are evaluated
paragraphs: An expression is code that produces a value. A literal such as 7.5m is an expression; so are a property access, a method call, and subtraction.
Evaluation happens before assignment. In varianceHours = recordedHours - scheduledHours, the subtraction produces a value and that result is assigned to varianceHours.

concept.title: Conversions should be visible when meaning changes
paragraphs: TimeSpan.TotalHours returns double. TimeClock converts that value to decimal because the example compares it with an explicitly base-10 schedule value.
The cast is not a promise of extra accuracy. It is an explicit change of numeric representation, so the code should make it easy to see and discuss.

lab.objective: Calculate and display the difference between scheduled and recorded hours using typed numeric variables.
lab.startingCondition: Session 02 is finished. Return to the real csharp-learn-with-ai repository; do not remain in csharp-learn-with-ai-practice. You will edit the existing console entry point at src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App/Program.cs. It currently runs the service workflow and prints Total hours worked, but it does not yet contain the deterministic eight-hour ClockEntry used by this lab.

steps.text: Return to the real repository and open src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App/Program.cs. Locate the final Console.WriteLine that prints Total hours worked. This confirms you are editing the real console application rather than the Session 01 practice copy.

reveals.title: Common navigation mistake
reveals.text: If the file contains only Console.WriteLine("Hello, World!"), you opened the practice project. The real Program.cs begins with dependency-injection setup and ends by printing Total hours worked.

steps.text: Immediately after the existing Total hours worked line, add the setup below. Treat it as provided context: it creates one entry that starts at 9:00 AM and ends exactly eight hours later. The numeric declarations remain your work.

reveals.title: What the setup guarantees
reveals.text: shiftStart.AddHours(8) produces a clock-out time eight hours after clock-in. Therefore entry.GetDuartion().TotalHours will produce 8 as a double.

steps.text: Before adding the three numeric variables, inspect the setup and write your predictions in a notebook or temporary comment. Assume scheduledHours will be 7.5m, recordedHours will come from the eight-hour entry, and varianceHours will mean recorded minus scheduled. Predict each resulting value and type. This makes your current mental model testable before the program gives you the answer.

reveals.title: Expected reasoning
items: scheduledHours should be decimal 7.5 because the schedule will be assigned the literal 7.5m.
recordedHours should be decimal 8.0 because clock-out is exactly eight hours after clock-in and TotalHours will be converted from double to decimal.
varianceHours should be decimal 0.5 because recorded minus scheduled is 8.0 - 7.5.

steps.text: Below the setup, declare scheduledHours explicitly as decimal and assign 7.5m. The m suffix matters because a fractional literal is double by default; here the schedule is deliberately a base-10 value.

reveals.title: Common mistake
reveals.text: Writing decimal scheduledHours = 7.5; does not compile because 7.5 is a double literal. Add the m suffix to make the literal decimal.

steps.text: On the next line, call entry.GetDuartion().TotalHours. TotalHours produces double, so cast that result to decimal and assign it to an explicitly typed recordedHours variable. Keep the cast beside the source so the representation change is visible.

reveals.title: Common mistakes
items: The existing method is intentionally spelled GetDuartion; GetDuration will not compile in this repository.
Removing (decimal) causes a conversion error because C# does not implicitly assign this double result to decimal.

steps.text: Create varianceHours by subtracting scheduledHours from recordedHours. Read the expression aloud as recorded minus scheduled, then compare the result with the prediction you wrote earlier.

reveals.title: Why order matters
reveals.text: Reversing the operands still compiles, but produces -0.5 and changes the meaning: it would calculate scheduled minus recorded.

steps.text: Print the three values. Use F2 for the first two lines so two decimal places are visible, and use the supplied positive/negative/zero format for variance. Run the console app, compare the three lines with your written prediction, and then run the tests to check that the existing behavior still passes.

reveals.title: Expected output
reveals.text: Ignore the earlier Total hours worked value for this exercise. The three deterministic lines should be:
reveals.code:
Scheduled hours: 7.50
Recorded hours: 8.00
Variance hours: +0.50

reveals.title: Common validation mistakes
items: A build error mentioning double and decimal usually means the m suffix or explicit cast is missing.
A variance of -0.50 means the subtraction order is reversed.
An exception saying the employee has not clocked out means ClockOutEmployee was omitted or placed after GetDuartion.
Different spacing is harmless; the three numeric values and the passing tests are what matter.

lab.expectedBehavior: After the existing Total hours worked line, the console reports 7.50 scheduled hours, 8.00 recorded hours, and a +0.50 variance. The student's written predictions match those values, the application exits without an exception, and all tests pass.
lab.validation: dotnet run --project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App.csproj --configuration Release && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release

expectedFiles.why: Add typed numeric values, an explicit conversion, and observable expressions.
Publish the synchronized lesson, scaffolded lab, hidden guidance, and quizzes.

commit: session-03: teach variables expressions and numeric types
review: Each variable name describes its role in the calculation.
Decimal literals use the m suffix.
The double-to-decimal conversion is explicit and close to its source.
The variance expression has an unambiguous subtraction order.
Output formatting does not change the stored numeric values.
The solution builds without warnings and all tests pass.

postQuiz.prompt: The output shows +0.50. Where is the plus sign introduced?
options: By the custom numeric format used for display
postQuiz.explanation: Formatting controls the text representation; the stored decimal value is still 0.5m.

postQuiz.prompt: What changes if scheduledHours becomes 8.5m while recordedHours remains 8m?
postQuiz.explanation: The expression is recorded minus scheduled, so a larger schedule produces a negative result.

postQuiz.prompt: Why not declare every numeric value as var in this lesson?
options: Explicit types keep the numeric contract visible while the concept is being learned
postQuiz.explanation: Type inference is useful, but explicit types make this lesson's conversions and numeric choices easier to inspect.

reflections: Which parts of the new statements are expressions?
What information does decimal communicate that the variable name alone does not?
Does formatting a value to two decimal places change the value or only its text representation?
whatBreaks: Removing scheduledHours leaves no comparison target. Removing the explicit conversion prevents assignment from double to decimal. Reversing the subtraction changes the meaning of positive and negative variance even though the code still compiles.
summary: Variables are typed names for values. Expressions produce values, literals have types, conversions change representation, and formatting changes only how a value is displayed.
